content: The MMR vaccine is a combination of live attenuated viruses designed to provide immunity against measles, mumps, and rubella. It is administered via injection, typically to children around the age of one year, with a booster dose given before they start school, usually at the age of four or five. In the United States, the practice of administering a booster dose began in the mid-1990s. Since its introduction in the 1970s, over 500 million doses of the MMR vaccine have been distributed in more than 60 countries. The vaccine is marketed under different names, including M-M-R II by Merck, Priorix by GlaxoSmithKline Biologicals, and TRIMOVAX by Sanofi Pasteur. Ongoing research continues to evaluate the long-term effects and efficacy of the vaccine. Before the introduction of the measles vaccine, the disease was so widespread that contracting it was considered almost inevitable. However, in countries with routine childhood vaccination programs, the incidence of measles has dropped to less than 1% among individuals under the age of 30. Vaccination has been shown to significantly reduce illness, disability, and mortality associated with measles. In the first 20 years of measles vaccination in the United States, it is estimated that 52 million cases of the disease, 17,400 cases of mental retardation, and 5,200 deaths were prevented. Between 1999 and 2004, a global vaccination strategy led by the World Health Organization and UNICEF averted an estimated 1.4 million measles-related deaths worldwide. Although measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, maintaining high vaccination rates and effective communication with vaccine-hesitant individuals are essential to prevent outbreaks. For example, in 2005, a single unvaccinated individual who contracted measles in Romania triggered an outbreak in a U.S. community with many unvaccinated children. This outbreak infected 34 people, most of whom were unvaccinated children, and resulted in 9% of cases requiring hospitalization. The cost of containing the outbreak was estimated at $167,685. High vaccination rates in surrounding communities helped prevent a larger epidemic. Mumps, another viral disease of childhood, was once very common. A rare but known complication of mumps is male sterility. Rubella, also known as German measles, was similarly widespread before vaccination became routine. The primary concern with rubella is its potential to cause congenital rubella syndrome in babies if a pregnant woman becomes infected, leading to severe congenital defects. All three diseases—measles, mumps, and rubella—are highly contagious. The combined MMR vaccine was developed to provide immunity against all three diseases with a single injection, reducing the pain and logistical challenges associated with administering three separate vaccines. In 2005, a Cochrane Library review of 31 studies concluded that while the effectiveness of mass immunization in eliminating these diseases is well-documented, no studies meeting their inclusion criteria directly assessed the vaccine's effectiveness. The review supported the continued use of the MMR vaccine for global measles eradication and reducing morbidity and mortality from mumps and rubella. The MMR vaccine is composed of live attenuated viral strains that are propagated in animal or human cells. For example, the measles and mumps virus strains are grown in embryonated hens' eggs and chick embryo cell cultures, resulting in strains that are less virulent to human cells. These are referred to as attenuated or neuroattenuated strains, as they are less harmful to human neurons compared to wild strains. The rubella component, known as Meruvax, is produced using a human cell line (WI-38) derived from embryonic lung tissue in 1961. The use of human cell lines has sparked some religious controversy. The vaccine is supplied in a freeze-dried (lyophilized) form and reconstituted with a solvent before administration. It is given via subcutaneous injection. High vaccination coverage before the age of two is critical, and a second booster dose is necessary to achieve adequate immunity and interrupt virus transmission. The booster dose can be administered as early as one month after the initial dose. Adverse reactions to the MMR vaccine are generally mild and rarely serious. Approximately 10% of children develop fever, malaise, and a rash 5–21 days after the first dose, while 5% experience temporary joint pain. Older women are at a higher risk of joint pain, acute arthritis, and, in rare cases, chronic arthritis. Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, is extremely rare. Neurological adverse events are also rare, though there is evidence linking the Urabe mumps strain in some MMR vaccines to cases of aseptic meningitis, a mild and transient form of viral meningitis. Due to these cases, the UK National Health Service discontinued the use of the Urabe strain in the early 1990s, replacing it with the Jeryl Lynn mumps strain. However, the Urabe strain is still used in some countries because it is cheaper to produce and has higher efficacy, despite a slightly higher rate of mild side effects. A Cochrane Library review highlighted issues with the quality of safety studies on the MMR vaccine and recommended standardized definitions for adverse events. The review concluded that while the design and reporting of safety outcomes in MMR studies are inadequate, the vaccine's role in preventing the target diseases outweighs the risks of adverse events. The MMR vaccine became the subject of controversy in the UK following a 1998 study by Andrew Wakefield and colleagues, which suggested a temporal association between the vaccine and autism spectrum disorders in 12 children. During a press conference, Wakefield proposed administering the vaccines as three separate doses rather than a single combined injection, although this suggestion was not supported by the study itself. Subsequent peer-reviewed research has consistently failed to find any link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Administering the vaccines separately does not reduce the risk of adverse effects and increases the likelihood of infection with the diseases not yet vaccinated against. Wakefield's study has been widely discredited on scientific and ethical grounds, and his actions have been criticized for contributing to a decline in vaccination rates. In 2004, ten of the study's twelve coauthors formally retracted the interpretation section of the paper. Major health organizations, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Institute of Medicine, the UK National Health Service, and the Cochrane Library, have all concluded that there is no evidence of a link between the MMR vaccine and autism. The MMRV vaccine, which combines the MMR vaccine with the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine, has been proposed as a replacement for the MMR vaccine to simplify vaccine administration.
